Lewis Structures Tell Us Connections. What About Shape?

Learning Objective: Connect a Lewis drawing to a three-dimensional molecular structure.
We drew H–O–H to count electrons. The straight line on the page did not mean that water is a linear molecule.
The atoms form a bent molecule. We need to consider all four electron groups around O.
Lewis structure → electron groups → 3D geometry → molecular polarity
Model key: atoms are solid spheres; sticks are bonds. Amber paired dots and translucent lobes mark schematic lone-pair regions. Element colors identify atoms, not positive or negative charge. Atoms: H white; C graphite; N blue; O red; F pink; Cl green; P violet; S yellow; Xe cyan.
Element colors stay constant: every H atom uses the same white material. Perspective, overlap and surface shading show depth; distance does not change the element color.
Integrated Slide 46 · Local Slide 2

Count Electron Groups, Not Bond Lines

Learning Objective: Count each bonded-atom direction and each central lone pair once.
Around the centerCounts as
A single bond to one atom1 electron group
A double or triple bond to one atom1 electron group
A lone pair on the central atom1 electron group
Electron groups = bonded atoms around the center + central lone pairs
CO₂: 2 groups. H₂O: 2 bonded atoms + 2 lone pairs = 4 groups. Terminal-atom lone pairs are not counted around the central atom. Formal charge counts bond lines; VSEPR counts regions.
Integrated Slide 47 · Local Slide 3

VSEPR: Make Room for Electron Groups

Learning Objective: Explain how electron-group repulsions lead to three-dimensional arrangements.
Valence-shell electron-pair repulsion theory = VSEPR
Electron-rich regions repel each other. Around a central atom, the groups arrange to reduce repulsions by spreading apart in three dimensions.
A bond angle is the angle between two bonds that meet at the central atom. VSEPR predicts a basic arrangement and approximate angles; the Lewis drawing itself does not fix the angle.
Integrated Slide 48 · Local Slide 4

Two Names Answer Two Different Questions

Learning Objective: Distinguish electron-group geometry from molecular geometry.
NameWhat is included?NH₃
Electron-group geometryAll bonding regions and central lone pairsTetrahedral
Molecular geometryThe positions of the atomsTrigonal pyramidal
NH₃: 3 bonding groups + 1 lone pair = 4 electron groups
Count all four electron groups to identify the tetrahedral arrangement. Look only at the three H atoms to name the molecular shape: trigonal pyramidal. With no central lone pairs, the electron-group geometry and molecular geometry have the same name.
Integrated Slide 49 · Local Slide 5

2 Electron Groups

Learning Objective: Count the bonding groups and central lone pairs to identify the molecular shape for 2 electron groups.
C is bonded to two O atoms. Each C=O counts as one group; C has no lone pairs.
The terminal oxygen lone pairs do not change the two-group count at C. Carbon has an octet even though it has only two electron groups.
Integrated Slide 50 · Local Slide 6

3 Electron Groups

Learning Objective: Count the bonding groups and central lone pairs to identify the molecular shape for 3 electron groups.
H₂CO has two C–H single bonds and one C=O double bond: three groups. SO₂ still has three groups in its resonance descriptions. Its two O atoms form a bent shape; the lone pair completes the electron-group arrangement.
Integrated Slide 51 · Local Slide 7

4 Electron Groups

Learning Objective: Count the bonding groups and central lone pairs to identify the molecular shape for 4 electron groups.
All three centers have four electron groups. Molecular geometry follows the atoms that remain after accounting for the lone pairs. NH₃ is not trigonal planar, and H₂O is not linear.
Integrated Slide 52 · Local Slide 8

Why Are the Angles Not All 109.5°?

Learning Objective: Separate ideal electron-group angles from actual molecular bond angles.
Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion
In these examples, lone pairs occupy more space near the center and compress the angles between bonds.
VSEPR gives an ideal reference angle, not one exact number for every molecule with that shape. A multiple bond still counts as one group, but can repel more strongly than a single bond. For example, H₂CO is planar without having three exactly equal 120° angles.

Five Groups: Axial and Equatorial Positions

Learning Objective: Identify the axial and equatorial positions in a five-group arrangement and compare their ideal angles.
Find the shaded equatorial plane. Three electron-group positions lie in this plane. The two axial positions are above and below it, perpendicular to the plane.
Five-group roadmap: PF₅ shows the three equatorial and two axial positions. We use the complete five-group chart on the next slide when lone pairs replace bonded atoms.
Axial: two opposite sites above and below the triangular plane. Equatorial: the three sites in the triangular plane.
Pair of directionsIdeal angle
Axial–equatorial90°
Equatorial–equatorial120°
Axial–axial180°
An axial group has three 90° neighbors; an equatorial group has two. This matters when one of the groups is a lone pair.
Integrated Slide 55 · Local Slide 11

Five Groups With Lone Pairs: Seesaw, T-Shaped, Linear

Learning Objective: Count the bonding groups and central lone pairs to identify the molecular shape for 5 electron groups.
The shaded plane contains all three equatorial positions, including any lone pairs. SF₄ has two F atoms and one lone pair in the plane; ClF₃ has one F atom and two lone pairs; XeF₂ has three lone pairs. The two remaining positions are above and below the plane.
Lone pairs prefer equatorial sites because they have fewer 90° interactions. In XeF₂, the three equatorial sites are lone pairs, leaving two opposite axial Xe–F bonds. A molecule with lone pairs can still be linear.
Integrated Slide 56 · Local Slide 12

6 Electron Groups

Learning Objective: Count the bonding groups and central lone pairs to identify the molecular shape for 6 electron groups.
Find the shaded square plane: four positions lie in one plane, with two more above and below. In ClF₅, one above/below position is a lone pair. In XeF₄, both above/below positions are lone pairs, leaving all four F atoms in the square plane. For SF₆, this plane is a drawing reference; its six positions are equivalent.
Four directions form a square plane; two more point above and below that plane. In XeF₄, the two lone pairs occupy opposite sites, leaving four F atoms in one square plane. Square planar is different from tetrahedral, even though both have four attached atoms.

More Than One Center: Analyze Each Atom Locally

Learning Objective: Apply VSEPR separately to each relevant center in a larger molecule.
Match O on the left, the middle CH₂ carbon, and the CH₃ carbon on the right in the two drawings. Each picture shows the same atom connections and viewing direction.
A larger molecule does not have one VSEPR label that describes every atom. Examine each center and the atoms directly attached to it.
CenterAttached atoms + central lone pairsLocal molecular geometry
CH₃ carbon4 + 0 = 4 groupsTetrahedral
CH₂ carbon4 + 0 = 4 groupsTetrahedral
O in –O–H2 + 2 = 4 groupsBent
The oxygen lone pairs are not included in the atom-only model, but they must be included in the count. Do not count all bonds or lone pairs in the molecule as though they surround one central atom.
Integrated Slide 58 · Local Slide 14

Bond Dipoles: Which Way Do Electrons Pull?

Learning Objective: Read a bond-dipole arrow and define the molecular dipole moment.
A bond-dipole arrow points toward the more electronegative, electron-rich end. Its crossed tail marks the electron-poor end.
Blue δ+ = partial positive · Red δ− = partial negative
The Greek letter μ (mu) denotes dipole moment: a measure of charge separation. The molecular dipole combines the effects of the entire molecular electron distribution.
For our neutral-molecule comparisons: μ = 0 → nonpolar; μ ≠ 0 → polar. We use the bond-arrow directions to reason about cancellation; no vector calculation or numerical dipole value is needed here.
Integrated Slide 59 · Local Slide 15

Polar Bonds: Cancel or Reinforce?

Learning Objective: Combine bond-dipole directions using the actual molecular shape.
CO₂ · bond dipoles cancel · μnet = 0 (no overall arrow)
H₂O · bond dipoles reinforce · overall arrow toward O
MoleculeBond directionsOverall result
CO₂Two equivalent C=O dipoles in opposite directionsCancel: nonpolar
H₂OTwo O–H dipoles at an angleDo not cancel: polar
The broad translucent arrow appears on the 3D H₂O model in this final Build and indicates the overall molecular dipole; individual bond arrows remain thin in the 2D drawings. H₂, Cl₂, and O₂ are nonpolar diatomic molecules because the identical atoms share equally. CO₂ shows a different route to a nonpolar molecule: its bonds are polar, but their contributions cancel in the linear arrangement.
Integrated Slide 60 · Local Slide 16

Symmetry Needs Matching Bond Dipoles

Learning Objective: Explain why tetrahedral does not automatically mean nonpolar.
MoleculeWhat can cancel?Polarity
CCl₄Four equal C–Cl dipoles in a tetrahedral arrangementNonpolar
CHCl₃Replacing one Cl with H changes the bond contributionsPolar
Identify the 3D arrangement and the attached atoms. Equivalent surrounding atoms can give complete cancellation in a symmetric arrangement. Different substituents require a fresh dipole check; shape alone is not enough.

Worked Example: OF₂ Is Bent, but O Is the Positive End

Learning Objective: Use electron count, geometry, and electronegativity together.
Total VE = 6 + 2(7) = 20 e⁻. Around O: 2 bonded atoms + 2 lone pairs = 4 groups → tetrahedral electron-group geometry, bent molecular geometry.
Given rounded EN values: O = 3.5 and F = 4.0. ΔEN = 0.5. Each bond arrow points from O toward F; the bent arrangement does not cancel the arrows.
OF₂ is [ _______ ]
The translucent net dipole is revealed over the 3D model at this final Build, pointing from the O-rich center toward the F side. Compare with H₂O: both molecules are bent, but F is more electronegative than O. Oxygen is the δ+ end in O–F, not automatically the negative end in every molecule.
Integrated Slide 62 · Local Slide 18

Lone Pairs Do Not Automatically Mean Polar

Learning Objective: Recognize cancellation in linear and square-planar molecules with lone pairs.
SpeciesMolecular geometryEquivalent bond-dipole result
XeF₂LinearTwo opposite Xe–F dipoles cancel: nonpolar
XeF₄Square planarTwo opposite pairs cancel: nonpolar
The lone pairs affect geometry, but their presence is not a stand-alone polarity test. For comparison, SF₄ (seesaw), ClF₃ (T-shaped), and ClF₅ (square pyramidal) are polar; PF₅ and SF₆ have symmetric cancellation and are nonpolar.

Ions: Charge Changes the Electron Count, Not the VSEPR Method

Learning Objective: Predict polyatomic-ion geometry from the complete Lewis electron count.
IonTotal VECentral groupsMolecular geometry
NH₄⁺5 + 4(1) − 1 = 84Tetrahedral
NO₃⁻5 + 3(6) + 1 = 243Trigonal planar
NO₂⁻5 + 2(6) + 1 = 183Bent
CO₃²⁻4 + 3(6) + 2 = 243Trigonal planar
Resonance does not add electron groups or make the molecule switch shapes. The nitrate/nitrite models show one contributor through the multiple sticks; the real ion has delocalized bonding. Here, report ion charge and geometry; our simple polar/nonpolar labels are being applied to neutral molecules.
Integrated Slide 64 · Local Slide 20

Resonance to 3D Shape: O₃ and NO₂⁻

Learning Objective: Connect complete resonance contributors to one bent atom arrangement, then distinguish neutral molecular polarity from bond-polarization reasoning for ions.
Recall T9.3: the atoms stay connected as electrons are delocalized. Compare both resonance contributors side by side; the central atom has one lone pair in each species.

O₃ · 18 valence e⁻

↔

NO₂⁻ · 18 valence e⁻

↔

O₃ · neutral molecule

NO₂⁻ · polyatomic ion

Both central atoms have three electron groups (two bonded directions + one lone pair): trigonal-planar electron-group geometry and bent molecular geometry. Bond orders are delocalized; front and oblique views depict the same nuclei from different viewpoints, not resonance switching. In oblique view, the rear O is drawn smaller/dimmer and the front O larger for depth clarity.
O₃: net molecular dipole

Central O has positive formal charge in each contributor; the terminal side carries more negative electron density. Although all O atoms have the same electronegativity, the resonance-delocalized charge distribution separates positive and negative electron density along the angle bisector; ozone is polar.

NO₂⁻: an ion, not a neutral-molecule polarity label

The N–O bonds are polarized toward O, but the ion has a net −1 charge. An absolute dipole moment for a charged species depends on the choice of origin; do not classify it as a neutral polar/nonpolar molecule.

Integrated Slide 65 · Local Slide 21

Put It Together: H₂CO Is Planar and Polar

Learning Objective: Follow the full Lewis → groups → geometry → polarity sequence.
Total VE = 2(1) + 4 + 6 = 12 e⁻
The C=O double bond is one direction, not two groups. Carbon has no lone pairs. The geometry is planar with angles near 120°, rather than three equal measured angles.
The atoms attached to C are O, H, and H. The strong C=O bond dipole is not canceled by the C–H contributions. H₂CO is polar. A planar molecule is not automatically nonpolar.
